body.text: So many knew something was seriously wrong with the conduct of some Australian special forces troops in Afghanistan, but they did little or nothing about it.

Senior officers knew some of their soldiers didn’t undergo mental health screening before and after multiple deployments to Afghanistan, leading to what an official report would later call “moral decay.” They knew discipline was degrading as the Afghan war dragged on. They knew of serious misconduct but didn’t investigate, and some might even have concealed it. They knew soldiers were planting weapons on dead Afghans. They knew Australians were killing a disproportionate number of Afghans but took no action.

What was known or suspected — and the failure to act on it — is revealed in the belated release of a summary of the findings of an official inquiry into the conduct of the special forces. The report highlights a “breakdown of command” in the governance and control of troops in war, an absence of effective leadership, and an erosion of discipline among soldiers who adopted an “uncontrolled warrior culture” and considered themselves “untouchable.”

It shows a military structure turned on its head, with captains and lieutenants subservient to lower-ranking sergeants and corporals whose “unhealthy appetite” for fighting was at odds with a strategy that aimed to win the support of the Afghan people.

The summary of the inquiry’s findings was posted on the website of the Inspector General of the Australian Defence Force, or IGADF, late last month, after the defence department twice refused to release the report to the Australian under freedom of information laws.

The report was commissioned following the 2020 release of the IGADF’s first inquiry, the Brereton Report, which found “credible evidence” that special forces troops murdered thirty-nine Afghan civilians and prisoners. Brereton found there was no evidence senior officers knew, or suspected, that troops were committing war crimes — a finding resented by some Afghan veterans who felt the lower ranks were being unfairly singled out. The second report is likely to fuel that resentment.

Brereton found that some officers might have had a “sense” that troops were using lethal force when “perhaps it was not always necessary” in the light of the number of “enemies” the troops were killing, some of whom were unarmed. But Brereton said this didn’t mean they knew or even suspected their troops were committing war crimes. At the same time, it didn’t relieve them of “all responsibility, as distinct from criminal responsibility.”

The second inquiry, kept secret since it was completed in 2022, was asked to identify any causal link between the “cultural context” in the Special Operations Task Group — the SOTG, made up of the Special Air Service Regiment, commandos and supporting troops — and “the prevalence of alleged unlawful behaviour unknown to or suspected by command.”
It found that while the cultural context didn’t cause serious misconduct, it “contributed to an environment that enabled misconduct to occur without timely detection.”

The second inquiry was also asked to “find out whether there were any things that could have been indicators to alert tactical, operational or strategic commanders to the possibility that SOTG members were potentially committing serious misconduct.”

Combined, Brereton and the subsequent inquiry reveal there were many “things,” multiple warning signs, that indicated something was seriously amiss with the conduct of a small number of soldiers, particularly in the Special Air Service Regiment. The second inquiry indicates commanders should have had more than a “sense” that something was amiss.

Clear signs were there, even though secrecy, restrictions on the flow of information and the “corruption” of internal reporting left higher command and ultimately the government with a “distorted view of operational conditions.” The second inquiry refers to suggestions this false internal reporting “was part of a broader ‘war’ against superior command in which higher headquarters were told what they wanted to hear, rather than what actually happened.”

Even so, the inquiry found: “Indicators of organisational decline, if not unlawful behaviour of the nature identified by the [first] IGADF Afghanistan Inquiry, were readily apparent. The incremental normalisation of these behaviours, over an extended period, went unchallenged. There was no effective external intervention.”

The failure to act on the warning signs is attributed in both inquiries to a voluntary “organisational blindness” and an “abandoned curiosity” to what was going on, particularly from 2009 until the end of Australia’s active combat role in Afghanistan in 2013. They refer to a gradual breakdown in the governance and command of the special forces, which had the effect of removing “barriers designed to protect ADF members from the moral harm attendant in combat operations.”

“It is striking how widely elements of decline were known, yet little effective or timely remedial action was taken,” the second report says. Senior officers, knew, for example, that the troops were killing an unusually large number of people referred to in military jargon as EKIA — enemy killed in action.

“There was tangible data available for higher headquarters through trends in growing numbers of Enemy Killed in Action,” the report says. “This included growth and spikes in these statistics over time, as well as features such as a lack of wounded insurgents (only deaths) and the lack of ADF casualties. By historical standards, elements of this data presented as most unusual. Some commanders were alert to this data and rumours that accompanied it while others were not, which may suggest an abandonment of curiosity.”

The report continues: “There is no suggestion that those aware of rumours were specifically complicit in the misconduct, however, it is extraordinary that no effective action was taken given the gravity of the matters the subject of rumours. The issues should have been escalated and effective action taken to investigate the matters or, at the least, look behind them. Such immediate action may have provided cause for Special Operations Command to reflect on the fitness of Special Forces units for deployment, including the cumulative impact of repeat deployments on moral and mental health.”

The newly released executive summary provides no enemy casualty figures. Nor has the ADF ever provided, during the war or since, detailed numbers or even estimates of enemies killed, although ADF media releases issued during the conflict sometimes referred to insurgent leaders “removed from the battlefield” in special forces’ operations.

I asked the Department of Defence whether it had collated casualty figures and if it would provide its “best estimate” of the numbers killed. Despite having seven days to reply, and despite repeated follow-up emails, the department’s media team did not provide a response.
Unofficial reports, however, have put approximate figures on the number of enemies killed by Australians.

In his book on the role of Australian special forces in Afghanistan, Find, Fix, Finish, the writer Ben McKelvey says the number of Afghans killed “legally or illegally” by Australian special forces was “thought to be about 11,000.” McKelvey said this week he was confident of the figure, which he said was given to him by a senior soldier in Special Operations Command.

Afghan veteran Heston Russell, a former commando officer, has also cited a figure of 11,000. In evidence to a Senate committee on Australia’s engagement in Afghanistan he complained that the achievements of the SOTG were being lost due to a focus on alleged civilian deaths.

“There were over 11,000 insurgents and terrorists killed, yet our legacy has come down to accusations of illegally killing thirty-nine civilians,” Russell said. “That is less than 0.04 per cent of those killed during the conduct of our operations in Afghanistan, yet we hear nothing of the 99.96 per cent of those operations that saw our Australian special forces demonstrate everything it means to embody the Australian spirit and values we readily lack here today.” (His maths is a bit out: on his figures, the correct percentages are 0.35 and 99.65.)

Prompted by Russell’s claims, the late Labor senator Kimberley Kitching asked the then chief of the defence force, General Angus Campbell, if the 11,000 figure was accurate and if he could provide the numbers of captured or killed in each year of the conflict. General Campbell took the question on notice, saying: “I’m just not sure [about] the quality of our records, particularly with regard to captured and killed early on. But we’ll see whatever we can find.”

The Department of Defence subsequently provided the following written answer to the committee: “Historically Defence has not published aggregated enemy casualty numbers, as this is not a measure of performance or effectiveness for the Australian Defence Force. Given the complexity of Australia’s mission in denying Afghanistan as a safe haven for international terrorism, and the nature of some air and land combat operations, accurate enemy casualty numbers are often difficult to obtain and are likely to be inaccurate.”
The answer was carefully crafted: while it said the department had not published figures it did not say whether it had collated figures, accurate or not.
If accurate, the figure of 11,000 Afghans killed would be extraordinary, given that just twenty-one members of the special forces were killed across the eight years they served in Afghanistan.

Australia’s American and other allies in the Afghan war haven’t released figures on the number of insurgent forces killed in the conflict, either, according to the Costs of War project at Brown University in the United States. The project has published figures showing 42,100 “opposition fighters” were killed in Afghanistan between 2001 and 2019. (Civilian deaths in the same period numbered 43,074.)

If McKelvey and Russell’s figure of 11,000 is correct, and the Brown University overall figure is correct, it would mean Australian troops killed about a quarter of all enemy forces killed in the war — an unlikely number, given that Australia’s contribution to the war peaked at around 1500 troops, including 300 special forces. By comparison, American troop numbers peaked at around 100,000, British numbers reached around 10,000, while Canada had around 3000. These three countries also suffered the greatest losses among foreign forces.

Chris Masters, the only journalist ever embedded with the Australian special forces in Afghanistan, has written extensively on their role in the conflict. While he’s played a central role in reporting evidence of war crimes, his writing is infused with respect for the overwhelming majority of Australian soldiers.

In his ground-breaking book No Front Line, Masters writes that the number of Afghan “enemy” killed by Australian troops, mostly by special forces, was between 4000 and 5000. He says special forces were involved in 3000 incidents referred to as “troops in contact” — that is, firefights with insurgents.

Masters’s numbers, while on the face of it more credible than the 11,000 figure, are still striking, even accounting for the fact the Australian troops had advantages that insurgents lacked — greater mobility, better communications, excellent training and overwhelming firepower. Masters told me there is probably no precise number of Afghans killed given that some troops submitted inaccurate “after-action reports” — an issue highlighted in the IGADF inquiries. He said he was confident, however, that his figure, based on commanding officers’ reports, was more reliable than claims of 11,000.

If accurate, the body count of 4000 shows a “kill ratio” — the number of enemy killed compared to Australian losses — of 190 enemy killed for every one of the twenty-one special forces killed in the war. As the second IGADF report noted, the tally of enemy killed was, by “historical standards… most unusual.”

While establishing precise numbers in any conflict is difficult, Australian troops in the Vietnam war also achieved what’s known as a favourable “kill ratio,” but nothing like what appears to have been the case in Afghanistan. A historical article on the Department of Veterans Affairs’ website outlines the record of one infantry battalion that killed about eighty-seven enemy soldiers for the loss of one Australian, with other battalions likely to have achieved comparable results.

A project by Vietnam veterans turned academic researchers recorded Australians being involved in more than 6000 combat incidents during the Vietnam war, in which they killed more than 4000 enemy soldiers. While the actual number is likely to be higher, to put it in context Australian troop numbers in the Vietnam war peaked at 8000, more than five times greater than the equivalent number for Afghanistan.

If an accurate number of Afghan deaths will likely never be known, the IGADF reports reveal Australian special forces troops kept unofficial “score boards” of kills, competed with other units for the highest “score,” and were heavily influenced by the behaviour of their American counterparts, who Brereton says had a disproportionate and unhealthy influence on the Australians.

The inquiry reports say the focus on killing emerged among an insular group of soldiers, many of them serving multiple four-to-six-month rotations in Afghanistan, influenced by corporals and sergeants who dominated the planning and conduct of “kill and capture” operations. The reports reveal these soldiers adopted a “warrior hero culture,” believing they were exceptional and exempt from army standards and policies.

Their focus on “kinetic” operations — those involving lethal force — ran against a counterinsurgency strategy that aimed to win the support of the Afghan people. Brereton refers to the experience of Afghans during SOTG raids: “It is plain that these were a terrifying experience for villagers, regardless of their affiliations. Such raids may sometimes have removed a Taliban leader or otherwise disrupted the insurgency in the short term, but many did not further the long-term counterinsurgency effort. Fundamental principles of counterinsurgency warfare were disregarded; in particular, local nationals were presumed to be hostile; and the winning of the hearts and minds of local nationals was not given priority.”

While a body count wasn’t an official measure of success, the Brereton report reveals some soldiers regarded it as their only “KPI.” The second report says this tendency increased over time, with evidence that latter rotations of special forces were “prosecuting missions” even when there was little intelligence to support them. “This suggests an unhealthy appetite had developed for fighting,” the report says.

“With each successive deployment the number of Afghanistan deaths and collateral damage increased,” it goes on. “Whether through enhanced insurgent activity, an unhealthy familiarity with the operating environment, or the presence of hubris, the inference could be drawn that appetites for kinetic operations grew at the expense of the winning over of the local population.”

A key question these inquiries raise is whether there has been, or will be, a reckoning for the senior officers who knew, or should have known, that there was something seriously wrong with the conduct of some special forces troops.

Asked about the second IGADF report in a Senate committee last month, the chief of the ADF, Admiral Mark Hammond, appeared keen to put what he referred to as “historical issues” behind him. He said the IGADF’s findings and recommendations “were actioned by my predecessors. All departmental actions relevant to that inquiry have been completed.”

Pressed by Greens leader David Shoebridge, Admiral Hammond said he was unable to say whether officers had been “exited from the service,” or faced any other punishment, but took the question on notice. Asked about what action had been taken when senior command received data on the number of Afghans killed, he took this on notice, too.

Defence industry minister Pat Conroy was slightly more forthcoming in an ABC interview on the same day as the Senate hearing. Like Admiral Hammond, he insisted the inquiries had led to cultural reforms within the ADF, with clearer lines of accountability, improved ethics, and clearer lines of reporting.

As for any consequences for commanders, Mr Conroy said none had been sacked but the career prospects of a number of senior officers had been “impacted,” and they had “exited the service” because “they clearly weren’t candidates for promotion.” This, he said, amounted to accountability.
It’s unlikely it’s a level of accountability that will appease veterans aggrieved at the focus on the actions of low-ranking soldiers.

There’s another key question implicitly raised but not addressed by these inquiries: whether there will be any reckoning for former government leaders on both sides of politics — prime ministers Howard, Rudd, Gillard and Abbott — who sent soldiers to an unwinnable war in which victory came to the side that endured the most pain rather than the side that inflicted it?

Perhaps prime ministers, too, were misled by false reporting, heard what they wanted to hear, were voluntarily blind, and insisted throughout the war, against all the evidence, that the troops were making progress and were, in Julia Gillard’s words, “lauded around the world for their capabilities.” Did prime ministers, too, abandon curiosity when they sent soldiers to kill and be killed? •
